name: Data Structures and Algorithms with the C++ STL: shared-mutex guarded vector (ConcurrentVector)
listed_description: Book technique: shared locking enables higher read throughput and minimal lock scope (book ch. 20, Thread Safety and Concurrency with the STL, Best practices in action).
reason: Code present (chapter20/04_bestpractices.cpp, a ConcurrentVector over std::vector with std::shared_mutex, one writer and one reader thread of 100 operations each) but it is a demo with no timing code and no baseline (no plain std::mutex vector); the book gives no numbers. Directional claim only.

name: Extreme C: macro-based loop unrolling (example 1.6)
listed_description: Book technique: variadic-macro loop unrolling avoids loop overhead at the cost of binary size (book ch. 1, Essential Features).
reason: ch01-essential-features/ExtremeC_examples_chapter1_6.c is present but only expands LOOP(...) into repeated printf calls of the argument names; it contains no timing and no loop to compare against, and the book gives no numbers. Directional claim only.

name: Extreme C: Unix domain sockets instead of TCP loopback (chapter 20 calculator)
listed_description: Book technique: Unix domain sockets preferred over network sockets for same-host IPC because of lower overhead (book ch. 19 and 20).
reason: ch20-socket-programming holds UDS and TCP server and client code (folders calcser, calcsvc, client, server plus types.h) but no benchmark or timing; I did not open the socket sources. The book gives a qualitative statement only, no numbers. Directional claim only.

name: GPU Programming with C++ and CUDA: shared-memory tree reduction for trapezoidal integration (chapter 6)
listed_description: Book technique: GPU shared-memory tree reduction for trapezoidal integration of 10 million speed samples (book ch. 6, Calculating numerical integrals and Reducing from many).
reason: Code present (ch6/3_trapezoidal_travel/trapezoidal_travel_basic.cu without reduction and trapezoidal_travel_gpu_reduce.cu with a per-block shared-memory reduction, both timing a CPU loop with std::chrono and the GPU with CUDA events) but the repo stores no results (ch6/readme.md has build steps only) and the book gives wording only: GPU and CPU times in the same order at 1,000,000 points, the reduction cutting GPU time by an order of magnitude. No timing figures reachable. Directional claim only.

name: GPU Programming with C++ and CUDA: zero-copy NumPy buffer pointers into a CUDA library from Python (chapter 9)
listed_description: Book technique: passing NumPy data pointers to a CUDA vector-add library instead of copying Python lists (book ch. 9, Passing numpy arrays to your library and Analyzing performance).
reason: Code present (ch9: CMake-built libvector_add, python/ctypes, python/wrapper and python/wrapper_np variants, run_tests.sh sweeping sizes from 1,000 to 10,000,000 with 10 runs each) but no results are stored in the repo; the book shows them only in a figure (Figure 9.2) and states thresholds in words (the list-copying wrapper wins at 100,000 elements or fewer, the NumPy-pointer wrapper beyond 1 million). The library is built with a CMake debug profile per the book. No numbers reachable. Directional claim only.

name: Hands-On Design Patterns with C++ 2nd ed: scoped_ptr and std::unique_ptr dereference versus raw pointer (chapter 5)
listed_description: Book technique: scoped_ptr and unique_ptr add no overhead over a raw pointer (book ch. 5, A Comprehensive Look at RAII).
reason: Code present (Chapter05/07_scoped_ptr_bm.C, Google Benchmark construct and dereference of raw pointer, scoped_ptr and unique_ptr) and the book numbers are 3.42, 3.37 and 3.42 ns per 32 dereferences, but this is a parity result: nobody claims the smart pointers are faster than the raw pointer, so there is no faster-than-baseline claim to catalogue.

name: Hands-On Design Patterns with C++ 2nd ed: local buffer optimization small_string (chapter 10)
listed_description: Book technique: small-string local buffer optimization (book ch. 10, Effect of local buffer optimization).
reason: Code present (Chapter10/04_small_string.C and 05_small_string.C) with numbers in the book (create a short string 18.7 ns against 835 ns per 32 creations, copy 53.5 against 786 ns, compare about 2x) but the baseline is the book's own simple_string, a strdup/free wrapper, not std::string (no std::string row exists in the benchmark, and std::string already has SSO). No named recognizable baseline.

name: Hands-On Design Patterns with C++ 2nd ed: small_vector local buffer optimization (chapter 10)
listed_description: Book technique: small_vector with an inline buffer, roughly 10x faster to create and copy small vectors (book ch. 10, Small vector).
reason: Code present (Chapter10/06_small_vector.C and 07_small_vector.C) but the baseline in the benchmark is the book's own simple_vector (malloc/free of an int array), not std::vector, and the benchmarks only create vectors (no copy benchmark in the opened files); the book gives 'roughly 10x' with no table in the text I was given. No named recognizable baseline and no timing figures.

name: Hands-On Design Patterns with C++ 2nd ed: smartptr_te_lb type-erased smart pointer with local-buffer deleter (chapter 10)
listed_description: Book technique: type-erased smart pointer whose deleter lives in a local buffer (book ch. 10, Type-erased and callable objects).
reason: Code present (Chapter10/09_smartptr.C) with book numbers of 21.0 ns static deleter, 44.2 ns type-erased and 22.3 ns type-erased with local buffer, but the baseline is the book's own heap-allocating type-erased pointer, not a standard facility. The std::shared_ptr comparison for the same idea is recorded as paper:book-hands-on-design-patterns-with-cpp-second-edition-local-buffer-smartptr.

name: Hands-On Design Patterns with C++ 2nd ed: type-erased local buffer with vtable (Buffer<S, A>) (chapter 10)
listed_description: Book technique: vtable-based type-erased local buffer (book ch. 10, Local buffer optimization in detail).
reason: Code present (Chapter10/10_local_buffer.C and 11_local_buffer_vtable.C) with book numbers of 5.45 ns without type erasure against 4.02 ns with the vtable version when copying a trivially copyable lambda, but the baseline is the same book buffer without type erasure, not std::any, std::function or another standard facility. No recognizable baseline.

name: Hands-On Design Patterns with C++ 2nd ed: thread-specific cache-line-aligned counters (chapter 18)
listed_description: Book technique: per-thread counters aligned to 64 bytes and merged once, instead of a mutex-guarded shared counter (book ch. 18, No sharing is the best sharing).
reason: Code present (Chapter18 examples 05 to 09; 06, 07 and 08 opened) but none of the opened files carries timing code and the book gives no timings. Directional claim only.

name: Hands-On Design Patterns with C++ 2nd ed: relaxed atomic counter and atomic index (chapter 18)
listed_description: Book technique: relaxed std::atomic increment instead of a mutex-protected counter (book ch. 18, Lock-free synchronization patterns).
reason: Code present (Chapter18/15_atomic_count.C and 16_atomic_index.C) but no timing code and no numbers in the book; the book only calls a mutex around a simple increment 'highly inefficient'. Directional claim only.

name: Hands-On Design Patterns with C++ 2nd ed: std::atomic_flag wait/notify (chapter 18)
listed_description: Book technique: C++20 std::atomic_flag wait and notify instead of a busy-polling loop (book ch. 18, Waiting patterns).
reason: Code present (Chapter18/12_wait_poll.C and 13_wait_notify_atomic.C) but no timing code and the book calls efficiency out of scope; it says only that the implementation is almost certainly more efficient than a polling loop. Directional claim only.

name: Hands-On Design Patterns with C++ 2nd ed: lock-free single-producer single-consumer fixed-array queue (chapter 18)
listed_description: Book technique: lock-free SPSC queue over a fixed array versus a mutex-protected queue (book ch. 18, Data structures with access limitations).
reason: Code present (Chapter18/21_lock_free_queue.C opened; 20_locked_queue.C is the mutex version) but no benchmark code (the only timing-related call is a 1 ns sleep to let the consumer catch up) and the book gives no numbers. Directional claim only.

name: Hands-On Design Patterns with C++ 2nd ed: C++20 coroutine generator versus hand-written iterator over a 3D array (chapter 18)
listed_description: Book technique: coroutine generator walking a 3D array compared with a hand-written state-machine iterator (book ch. 18, Coroutine patterns in C++, Example 28).
reason: Code and timing present (Chapter18/28_generator_coro.C times both with std::chrono::system_clock and checks the values) and the book numbers are mixed: Clang 17 iterator 9.2e-10 s against generator 6.4e-10 s per element, GCC 13 iterator 6.5e-10 s against generator 2.0e-9 s (about 3x slower). The generator is not claimed faster in general and the baseline is the book's own hand-written iterator, not a standard facility, so there is no faster-than-named-baseline claim.
